q: "Unlike his talkative brother, Bilal was reticent and rarely shared his opinions in class." In this sentence, 'reticent' most nearly means:
x: The contrast clue 'unlike his talkative brother' and the phrase 'rarely shared his opinions' show that reticent means reserved, not inclined to speak. Nothing in the sentence suggests rudeness or carelessness.

q: Choose the word that best fits: "The little boy ___ secretly through the gap in the curtain to see who was at the door."
x: To peep is to look quickly and secretly through a small opening, which matches 'secretly through the gap'. Stare and gaze suggest long open looking, and glare suggests anger.

q: "The fame of most social media stars is ephemeral; a video that is popular on Monday is forgotten by Friday." The word 'ephemeral' means:
x: The clause after the semicolon explains the word: popular on Monday, forgotten by Friday. So ephemeral means lasting a very short time. Permanent is the opposite.

q: Choose the word that best fits: "Exhausted and dizzy after the race, the runner ___ towards the finish line, almost falling twice."
x: To stagger is to walk unsteadily, as if about to fall, which fits 'exhausted and dizzy' and 'almost falling'. Strolled is relaxed, while marched and strode are firm and confident.

q: "Fatima was so meticulous that she checked every figure in the report three times before submitting it." The word 'meticulous' means:
x: Checking every figure three times is the example clue: meticulous means showing great care about small details. Nothing in the sentence shows speed, worry or pride.

q: Choose the word that best fits: "The gang leader was ___ throughout the district for his cruelty."
x: All four words mean 'well known', but notorious means famous for something bad, which suits cruelty. Renowned, celebrated and distinguished are used for admirable fame.

q: "Living on a small pension, Hamza's grandfather was frugal: he mended his old shoes rather than buy new ones and never wasted food." 'Frugal' means:
x: The examples after the colon (mending old shoes, never wasting food) show that frugal means careful and economical in spending. Greedy, careless and generous do not fit these examples.

q: Choose the word that best fits: "Even at eighty, Nani has a ___ sense of wonder, delighting in every bird and flower she sees."
x: Childlike has a positive shade: innocent and fresh like a child, which matches 'delighting in every bird'. Childish, immature and infantile are negative, suggesting silly behaviour.

q: "The instructions were so ambiguous that half the students answered one question and half answered another." The word 'ambiguous' means:
o: Open to more than one meaning
x: Students understood the same instructions in two different ways, which is the clue that ambiguous means having more than one possible meaning. Length or falseness would not explain the split.

q: Choose the correct version of this sentence: "After lunch, Grandfather lays down for an hour."
o: After lunch, Grandfather lays down for an hour.
After lunch, Grandfather lie down for an hour.
Yesterday after lunch, Grandfather laid down for an hour.
After lunch, Grandfather lies down for an hour.
x: 'Lie' (lie, lay, lain) means to rest and takes no object; 'lay' (lay, laid, laid) means to put something down and needs an object. So he 'lies down' now, and yesterday he 'lay down', not 'laid down'.

q: "The once-busy telegraph office now stands empty; the service became obsolete after mobile phones arrived." 'Obsolete' means:
x: The office 'now stands empty' because a newer technology replaced it, so obsolete means out of date and no longer used. Very popular is the opposite of what the clue shows.

q: The doctor gave me some useful ____ about my diet.
x: 'Advice' is the noun and is uncountable, so it has no plural 'advices'. 'Advise' is the verb, as in 'The doctor advised me'.

q: "After the long journey, Ayesha felt so lethargic that she could barely lift her school bag, let alone run for the bus." 'Lethargic' means:
x: Being barely able to lift a bag, let alone run, shows a lack of energy, so lethargic means sluggish and tired. Excited and restless is the opposite; calm does not explain the weakness.

q: The new rule will ____ all the students of the college.
x: 'Affect' is the verb meaning 'to have an influence on'. 'Effect' is usually the noun (the result), and 'affection' and 'effective' are a noun and an adjective.

q: "Mobile phones have become ubiquitous; you see them in villages, classrooms, hospitals and even at funerals." The word 'ubiquitous' means:
x: The list of very different places where phones are seen is the example clue: ubiquitous means present everywhere. The sentence says nothing about cost, usefulness or newness.

q: The ____ of our college addressed the students on the first day.
x: 'Principal' means the head of a school or college. 'Principle' means a rule or belief, and 'principled' is an adjective.

q: "The witness gave such a lucid account of the accident that the police had no difficulty understanding exactly what had happened." 'Lucid' means:
x: The result clause 'no difficulty understanding' shows that a lucid account is clear and easily understood. A brief, incomplete account would have caused difficulty.

q: "Planting trees along the roads can mitigate the heat of summer, making the streets a few degrees cooler." The word 'mitigate' means:
x: The phrase 'making the streets a few degrees cooler' shows the heat is reduced, so mitigate means make less severe. Increase is the opposite meaning.

q: "Far from being indolent, the new clerk arrived early, worked through lunch and was the last to leave." The word 'indolent' means:
x: 'Far from being' signals a contrast: the clerk's behaviour is the opposite of indolent. Since he is hardworking, indolent must mean lazy. Hardworking is the trap, because it describes the clerk, not the word.

q: "The obsequious waiter bowed every few seconds, agreed with everything the rich guest said and laughed loudly at all his jokes." 'Obsequious' means:
x: Constant bowing, agreeing with everything and laughing at every joke all show excessive eagerness to please someone important. That is the meaning of obsequious; the other options contradict the examples.

q: "The old man was too feeble to climb the stairs without help." The closest synonym of 'feeble' is:
x: Feeble means lacking physical strength, i.e. weak; that is why he needs help on the stairs. Lazy suggests unwillingness, not inability.

q: "Hira gave a candid answer: she admitted that she had not read the book at all." In this sentence, 'candid' most nearly means:
x: Admitting openly that she had not read the book shows that a candid answer is frank and honest. Nothing in the sentence suggests rudeness or hesitation.

q: "A diligent student, Usman revised every evening and never missed a class." In this sentence, 'diligent' most nearly means:
x: Revising every evening and never missing a class are signs of steady effort, so diligent means hardworking. Talent is not shown by these examples.

q: "Even after twenty years, my grandmother has a vivid memory of the day she first saw the sea, down to the colour of the sky." In this sentence, 'vivid' most nearly means:
x: She still remembers small details such as 'the colour of the sky', so a vivid memory is clear and detailed. Faint and blurred is the opposite.

q: "Copying the same table into fifty registers by hand was so tedious that the clerk kept checking the clock." In this sentence, 'tedious' most nearly means:
x: Repeating the same copying fifty times and watching the clock show the work was boring and tiring, which is what tedious means. The task was repetitive, not hard to understand.

q: "The resilient little town was flooded twice in ten years, yet each time its shops reopened within weeks." In this sentence, 'resilient' most nearly means:
x: 'Yet each time its shops reopened within weeks' shows the town bounced back after each disaster, so resilient means quick to recover. Being flooded twice does not make it 'easily damaged' in the sense of the word.

q: "Before signing the contract, the lawyer scrutinized every clause, reading some lines three or four times." In this sentence, 'scrutinized' most nearly means:
x: Reading some lines three or four times is the clue: to scrutinize is to examine something closely and carefully. Signing quickly is the opposite of what the lawyer did.

q: "In a hall full of people in dark suits, Sana's bright yellow scarf made her conspicuous." In this sentence, 'conspicuous' most nearly means:
x: A bright yellow scarf among dark suits stands out, so conspicuous means easily seen or noticed. The sentence says nothing about her feelings, so embarrassed is not supported.

q: "The rain has been sporadic this month: a short shower on the third, another on the twentieth, and nothing in between." In this sentence, 'sporadic' most nearly means:
x: The details after the colon show rain falling only now and then, with long gaps, so sporadic means occasional and irregular. Continuous is the opposite.

q: "Zain was apprehensive about the interview; he slept badly and kept imagining questions he could not answer." In this sentence, 'apprehensive' most nearly means:
x: Sleeping badly and imagining questions he could not answer show fear about what is coming, so apprehensive means worried or anxious. Excited would not explain the bad sleep and the fear of failing.

q: "The eloquent speaker held the audience's attention for an hour, choosing every word so well that no one looked away." In this sentence, 'eloquent' most nearly means:
x: 'Choosing every word so well' and holding attention for an hour show skill with language, which is what eloquent means. Nothing suggests anger or shyness.

q: "Rather than waiting for a perfect plan, the pragmatic headmistress fixed the leaking roof with what money she had." In this sentence, 'pragmatic' most nearly means:
x: She dealt with the problem sensibly using the means available instead of waiting for a perfect plan, so pragmatic means practical. Idealistic is the trap: an idealist would wait for the perfect plan, which 'rather than' rules out.

q: "Shouting at a frightened child only exacerbates the problem; he becomes more upset, not less." In this sentence, 'exacerbates' most nearly means:
x: The second clause, 'he becomes more upset, not less', shows the problem grows, so exacerbate means make worse. Solves is the opposite of this meaning.

q: "During the monsoon, water is abundant in the hills, and every stream is full." In this sentence, the word most nearly opposite in meaning to 'abundant' is:
x: Abundant means existing in large amounts, as 'every stream is full' shows; its opposite is scarce. Plentiful is a synonym, not an opposite.

q: "The boy tried to conceal the broken vase behind the sofa." In this sentence, the word most nearly opposite in meaning to 'conceal' is:
x: To conceal is to hide something, as the boy does by putting the vase behind the sofa; the opposite is to reveal it. Hide has the same meaning.

q: "The museum displays ancient coins that farmers found while ploughing their fields." In this sentence, the word most nearly opposite in meaning to 'ancient' is:
x: Ancient means belonging to the distant past, so its opposite is modern. Old is close in meaning, and rare and valuable describe other qualities.

q: "Pack the glasses carefully in newspaper; they are very fragile." In this sentence, the word most nearly opposite in meaning to 'fragile' is:
x: Fragile means easily broken, which is why the glasses need careful packing; its opposite is sturdy, strong and hard to break. Delicate is a synonym.

q: "Despite winning the national prize, the young scientist remained humble and thanked her teachers first." In this sentence, the word most nearly opposite in meaning to 'humble' is:
x: Humble means not thinking oneself better than others, as shown by thanking her teachers first; the opposite is arrogant. Modest is a synonym.

q: "Ahmed was reluctant to lend his new bicycle and agreed only after his mother insisted." In this sentence, the word most nearly opposite in meaning to 'reluctant' is:
x: Reluctant means unwilling, which is why he agreed 'only after his mother insisted'; the opposite is eager. Unwilling is a synonym, the trap for a hasty reader.

q: "The timid kitten hid under the bed whenever visitors came." In this sentence, the word most nearly opposite in meaning to 'timid' is:
x: Timid means easily frightened and shy, as hiding under the bed shows; the opposite is bold. Shy has nearly the same meaning.

q: "His directions were so vague that we drove around the market for an hour looking for the shop." In this sentence, the word most nearly opposite in meaning to 'vague' is:
x: Vague directions are unclear, which is why they got lost; the opposite is precise, meaning exact and clear. Unclear is a synonym.

q: "The villagers were hostile to the plan to build a factory on their farmland and protested every day." In this sentence, the word most nearly opposite in meaning to 'hostile' is:
x: Hostile to a plan means strongly against it, as the daily protests show; the opposite is favourable, meaning in support of it. Opposed is a synonym.

q: "When the road became wide and empty, the driver accelerated." In this sentence, the word most nearly opposite in meaning to 'accelerated' is:
x: To accelerate is to go faster, which an empty road allows; the opposite is to slow down. Sped up has the same meaning.

q: "Attendance at the morning assembly is compulsory; students who miss it must explain why." In this sentence, the word most nearly opposite in meaning to 'compulsory' is:
x: Compulsory means required by a rule, which is why absent students must explain; its opposite is optional, left to one's choice. Required is a synonym.

q: "Our new timetable is flexible, so students can choose when to take their breaks." In this sentence, the word most nearly opposite in meaning to 'flexible' is:
x: A flexible timetable can be changed to suit people, as the free choice of breaks shows; the opposite is rigid, fixed and unchangeable. Adaptable is a synonym.

q: "The council promised a transparent process, with every bid and every price published online." In this sentence, the word most nearly opposite in meaning to 'transparent' is:
x: Here transparent means open for everyone to see, as publishing every bid shows; the opposite is secretive. Open is a synonym.

q: "The report gave only a superficial account of the problem, mentioning the floods but never asking why they happened." In this sentence, the word most nearly opposite in meaning to 'superficial' is:
x: A superficial account deals only with the surface, never going into causes; the opposite is thorough, covering a matter fully and in depth. Shallow is a synonym.

q: "A cautious man with money, my uncle never put all his savings into one business." In this sentence, the word most nearly opposite in meaning to 'cautious' is:
x: Cautious means careful to avoid risk, as not putting all his savings in one place shows; the opposite is reckless. Careful is a synonym.

q: "The cloth merchants of the old city were prosperous, with large houses and many servants." In this sentence, the word most nearly opposite in meaning to 'prosperous' is:
x: Large houses and many servants show that prosperous means rich and successful; the opposite is impoverished, meaning very poor. Wealthy is a synonym.

q: "The new principal is lenient; she lets late students into class with only a warning." In this sentence, the word most nearly opposite in meaning to 'lenient' is:
x: Letting late students in with only a warning shows that lenient means mild in applying rules; the opposite is strict. Tolerant is close in meaning, not opposite.

q: "As a novice, Hamid needed help even to set up the chessboard." In this sentence, the word most nearly opposite in meaning to 'novice' is:
x: A novice is a beginner, which is why he needs help with the basics; the opposite is an expert. Beginner is a synonym.

q: "The poem was written by an obscure village poet whom few people have heard of." In this sentence, the word most nearly opposite in meaning to 'obscure' is:
x: 'Whom few people have heard of' shows that obscure here means not well known; the opposite is famous. Unknown is a synonym, and the word's other meaning, 'hard to understand', does not fit this sentence.

q: "The noise of the traffic diminished as we walked deeper into the forest." In this sentence, the word most nearly opposite in meaning to 'diminished' is:
x: To diminish is to become smaller or weaker, as noise does when we move away from the road; the opposite is to increase. Faded is close to a synonym.

q: "Fishermen often exaggerate the size of the fish that got away." In this sentence, the word most nearly opposite in meaning to 'exaggerate' is:
x: To exaggerate is to make something seem bigger than it really is; the opposite is to understate, to make it seem smaller or less important. Overstate is a synonym.

q: "The volcano has been dormant for centuries, but scientists still watch it closely." In this sentence, the word most nearly opposite in meaning to 'dormant' is:
x: Dormant means temporarily inactive, as if asleep, which is why it is still watched; the opposite is active. Inactive is a synonym.

q: "The verbose report ran to ninety pages when ten would have been enough." In this sentence, the word most nearly opposite in meaning to 'verbose' is:
x: Ninety pages where ten would do shows that verbose means using more words than needed; the opposite is concise, brief but complete. Wordy is a synonym.

q: "The benevolent landlord lowered the rent for families who had lost their jobs." In this sentence, the word most nearly opposite in meaning to 'benevolent' is:
x: Benevolent means kind and wishing good to others, as lowering the rent shows; the opposite is malevolent, wishing harm to others. Kind is a synonym.

q: "The school will not condone cheating of any kind; every case is reported to the board." In this sentence, the word most nearly opposite in meaning to 'condone' is:
x: To condone is to accept or excuse wrongdoing, which the school refuses to do; the opposite is to condemn, to say firmly that it is wrong. Excuse is close to a synonym.

q: Choose the word or phrase that best fits: "The shop near our college sells pens, paper, envelopes and other ___."
x: 'Stationery' means writing materials such as pens and paper. 'Stationary' means not moving, which does not fit a list of things for sale.

q: Choose the word or phrase that best fits: "She blushed when her teacher paid her a ___ on her neat handwriting."
x: A 'compliment' is a remark of praise, and we 'pay someone a compliment'. A 'complement' is something that completes or goes well with another thing.

q: Choose the word or phrase that best fits: "Please ___ this small gift as a token of our thanks."
x: 'Accept' means to take something that is offered. 'Except' means 'not including', and 'expect' means to think something will happen.

q: Choose the word or phrase that best fits: "These trousers are too ___; I need a belt to keep them up."
x: 'Loose' is an adjective meaning not tight, which is why a belt is needed. 'Lose' is a verb meaning to be unable to find something, and 'loss' is a noun.

q: Choose the word or phrase that best fits: "This small car is very ___; it uses little petrol even on long journeys."
x: 'Economical' means not wasting money or fuel, which fits 'uses little petrol'. 'Economic' means connected with the economy, as in 'economic growth'.

q: Choose the word or phrase that best fits: "After the meal, the guests were served kheer for ___."
x: 'Dessert' (double s) is the sweet dish at the end of a meal. 'Desert' is a dry, sandy region or a verb meaning to abandon.

q: Choose the word or phrase that best fits: "___ English, Ali speaks Urdu, Punjabi and Pashto."
x: 'Besides' means 'in addition to': Ali speaks English and these other languages too. 'Beside' means 'next to', and 'despite' and 'although' show contrast, which the sentence does not.

q: Choose the word or phrase that best fits: "My skin is very ___ to the sun and burns within minutes."
x: 'Sensitive' means easily affected or harmed, which fits skin that burns quickly. 'Sensible' means wise and practical, a common confusion.

q: Choose the word or phrase that best fits: "The ___ child turned an empty cardboard box into a spaceship."
x: 'Imaginative' describes a person with a strong, creative imagination. 'Imaginary' means not real, which would make the child unreal.

q: Choose the word or phrase that best fits: "The final match was ___ because of the heavy rain."
x: 'Call off' means to cancel, which suits a match stopped by rain. 'Call on' means to visit or ask someone to speak, and 'call for' means to demand.

q: Choose the word or phrase that best fits: "The police have promised to ___ the shopkeepers' complaint about the thefts."
x: 'Look into' means to investigate, which is what the police do with a complaint. 'Look after' means to take care of, and 'look up to' means to admire.

q: Choose the word or phrase that best fits: "She ___ the job offer because the office was too far from her home."
x: 'Turn down' means to refuse an offer, which the reason 'too far from her home' explains. 'Turn up' means to arrive or appear.

q: Choose the word or phrase that best fits: "The doctor advised my uncle to ___ smoking at once."
x: 'Give up' means to stop doing a habit. 'Give in' means to surrender, and 'give away' means to hand something over for free.

q: Choose the word or phrase that best fits: "Many young doctors ___ from their home country every year to work abroad."
x: To 'emigrate' is to leave one's own country to live in another, and it takes 'from'. To 'immigrate' is to come into a new country, so it would take 'to' or 'into'; 'emigrant' is a noun.

q: Choose the word or phrase that best fits: "Dark clouds and a sudden strong wind warned the fishermen that a storm was ___."
x: 'Imminent' means about to happen, which fits the warning signs. 'Eminent' means famous and respected, as in 'an eminent scientist'.

q: Choose the word or phrase that best fits: "Of tea and coffee, I prefer the ___, because tea keeps me awake at night."
x: 'The latter' means the second of two things named, here coffee; the reason shows the speaker does not want tea. 'The former' would mean tea, which the reason rules out, and 'later' refers to time.

q: Choose the word or phrase that best fits: "Only medical ___ are allowed inside the operating theatre."
x: 'Personnel' (stress on the last syllable) means the people employed in an organisation, here medical staff. 'Personal' is an adjective meaning private or one's own.
